rulings.Case Title: IN THE MATTER OF THE LIVING TRUST OF CERALINA HAFALIA TRUST
rulings.Calendar Matter: Notice Of Motion And Motion To Disqualify Respondent'S Counsel
rulings.Rulings: [Part 1 of 2] This tentative ruling is issued by Judge Michael B. McNaughton. Before the court is Petitioner James Hafalia's Motion to Disqualify Respondent's Counsel ("Motion"). Per the Notice of Motion and Memorandum of Points and Authorities, the Motion is brought pursuant California Rules of Professional Conduct, Rule 1.18, and Code of Civil Procedure section 128(a)(5). The Motion is DENIED, as follows. Petitioner has not caried his burden to show that disqualification of Respondent's counsel is appropriate under Rule 1.18. Under subsection (c), "A lawyer [who has communicated with a prospective client] shall not represent a client with interests materially adverse to those of a prospective client in the same or a substantially related matter if the lawyer received from the prospective client information protected by Business and Professions Code section 6068, subdivision (e) and rule 1.6 that is material to the matter, except as provided in paragraph (d)." Rule 1.18 requires Petitioner to "establish that (a) [he] was a prospective client, (b) that [he] communicated confidential information to an attorney and (c) the confidential information was either made public or disclosed to a third party." (Syre v. Douglas (2024) 104 Cal. App. 5th 280, 295.) As stated in Syre v. Douglas (2024) 104 Cal. App. 5th 280, 297, under Rule 1.18 "a prospective client is not elevated to the status of a former client and representation of a new client is not barred unless the attorney obtained information from the prospective client that could be significantly harmful to that person in the matter. (Rule 1.18, Com. [1][.)]" Disqualification under Rule1.18 is not required unless that is a showing of an exchange of actual confidential information. Unlike representation of a former client, where there is a conclusive presumption the attorney possesses confidential information, unless the attorney was formally retained following the initial consultation there is no presumption that the attorney possesses the prospective client's confidential information. (See, Med-Trans Corp., Inc. v. City of California City (2007) 156 CA4th 655, 668; Syre v. Douglas (2024) 104 Cal. App. 5th 280, 297). On the present record, Petitioner has not established that he communicated confidential information to Mr. Kithas in their initial prospective client conversation, which they agree was telephonic, lasted approximately ten minutes and did not result in Petitioner retaining Mr. Kithas' legal services in this matter. The only evidence of "confidential" information communicated in that prospective client conversation is a conclusory statement in Petitioner's declaration, at paragraph 4: "As I can recall, during the consultation with Mr. Kithas, I shared information related to the issues underlying my [Petition]. I shared confidential information, including my case theory, anticipated evidence, perceived strengths and weakness, other personal information potentially pertinent to the case and litigation goals." The court cannot accept a conclusory statement as evidence. Petitioner's offer, in paragraph 4 of his declaration, to file a further, "confidential" declaration in support of the Motion is denied, without prejudice to Petitioner bringing a motion to seal such a declaration and, if that motion is granted, presenting that sealed declaration in a second motion to disqualify Mr. Kithas as Respondent's counsel. Petitioner would bear the usual statutory burdens on any motion to seal, and on any further motion to disqualify opposing counsel.
